title: Unbroken by Trouble
note: He defines this as keeping the mind steady when trouble comes to someone striving at a task, whether it comes from god, from lack of wealth or from the strain on the body.

couplets.plain: Laugh when trouble comes. Nothing presses on it and rides it down like that.
couplets.pm: When your work brings you trouble, don’t break, but rejoice inside. Nothing else can press down on trouble again and again like that joy. Bring to the trouble the joy that belongs to finishing the work. Then you stay unbroken, your rising spirit thrusts it aside, and you have the strength to complete the task.

links.reason: Makes laughter the strongest stand one can take against trouble.
Gives someone beset by trouble a plain first move: meet it laughing.

couplets.plain: Even a flood of trouble dies away once a wise person sets their mind to it.
couplets.pm: Troubles shoreless as a flood all perish the moment a wise man thinks one thought in his mind. Suffering is nothing but a stance held in the mind, and it goes when that stance is reversed. He must know this, so he is called wise. “Thinks in his mind” shows how easy the means is.

links.reason: A wise mind, once set to it, makes even a flood of trouble die away.

links.remove: The image in the Tamil is a flood, வெள்ளம், not the sea. The sea is the old English.

links.quote: Even a flood of trouble dies away

couplets.plain: Those who aren’t troubled by trouble will give trouble trouble.
couplets.pm: Those not distressed by the trouble that comes in the middle of their work bring trouble on the trouble. Distress here means thinking of weakening and giving up. With a firm mind they keep striving, the work is finished and bears fruit, and then every trouble is gone. Take the next two couplets the same way.

couplets.plain: Trouble itself is in trouble when it meets someone who, like an ox, pulls through every blocked place.
couplets.pm: One who takes up the work and carries it through every obstacle, as an ox drags a cart through mire, leaves the trouble that comes to him in trouble itself. The ox scrapes its sides, plants its muzzle and crawls on its legs to drag the load through. So he strives, not minding the pain in his body.

links.quote: like an ox, pulls through every blocked place
links.reason: Pulling through every blocked place like an ox leaves the trouble itself in trouble.

couplets.plain: Even if they come heaped one on another, the troubles that reach an unbroken person are themselves in trouble.
couplets.pm: Even if they come without a break, the same one many times or different ones mixed, the troubles that reach one who holds to his resolve are themselves caught in trouble and pass away.

links.quote: the troubles that reach an unbroken person
links.reason: One who stays unbroken as troubles pile up leaves the troubles themselves in trouble.

links.quote: Even if they come heaped one on another
links.reason: Fits trouble piling on trouble: stay unbroken and it is the troubles that suffer.

couplets.plain: Will those who never clung to what they gained, saying “We have got it,” grieve and say “We have lost it”?
couplets.pm: In poor times, will they suffer in their minds, saying “We have become poor”? These are people who in rich times never knew how to cling, saying “We have got this.” They kept that temper when they gained, and they keep it when all is gone, so they have no grief. This is how to stand against trouble from lack of wealth.

links.quote: never clung to what they gained
links.reason: Whoever never clung to gain has no reason to cry out at loss.

couplets.plain: Those who know the body is a target for suffering don’t treat the turmoil that comes on them as distress.
couplets.pm: The wise see clearly that bodies, in all four states of birth, are targets for the sword of suffering. So they don’t take the suffering that comes on them as suffering, but accept it as natural. Some read கையாறு as a path of conduct.

links.quote: the body is a target for suffering

couplets.plain: Someone who doesn’t crave pleasure, and says suffering is natural, never comes to sorrow.
couplets.pm: One who wants no pleasures for his body, and is clear that work naturally brings suffering, doesn’t come to sorrow through his effort. Wanting pleasure brings sorrow, and so does refusing to call suffering natural and trying to ward it off. He has done neither.

links.reason: Taking suffering as natural removes its power to bring sorrow.

couplets.plain: Someone who doesn’t crave joy in times of joy won’t feel sorrow in times of sorrow.
couplets.pm: One who, when his work brings joy, lives through it without wanting it in his mind also lives through sorrow, when it comes, without grieving in his mind. Sorrow here means the trouble that comes with effort. He takes both as the same, so neither has any effect on him.

links.quote: won’t feel sorrow in times of sorrow

couplets.plain: If you take what hurts as joy, you will have the distinction your enemies prize.
couplets.pm: If, when you do your work, you make yourself treat the suffering of effort as joy, you gain the quality that makes your enemies respect you. Suffering isn’t natural to the soul. It is a passing stance in the mind. Reverse it and you stay unbroken and glad, with the strength to finish what you began.
couplets.sensitive: counsel to take pain as joy could reach someone enduring mistreatment

ideaLinks.quote: Someone who doesn’t crave joy in times of joy won’t feel sorrow in times of sorrow.
ideaLinks.reason: One who doesn’t crave joy in times of joy is spared sorrow in times of sorrow.
